chapter_theme: Poems 201 to 220 are of two kinds. 201 to 211 are bards' gift poems that test the terms of patronage: a poet offering a dead patron's daughters, poets leaving patrons who gave without regard or kept them waiting, and the bard's household as evidence. 212 to 220 follow Kopperuncholan and his unseen friend Pisirandhaiyar from praise and counsel through the king's resolve to die to the laments for him.

201.reading: Kapilar tells Irungovel that the girls with him are the daughters of Pari of Parambu, who gave his chariot to a jasmine creeper, that he himself, a brahmin poet and their father's friend, has brought them, and asks the lord of Thuvarai, chief of forty-nine generations of Velir, to take them as his gift.
201.nuance: The poet makes the girls his own gift (யான்தர), so a request for a bridegroom is cast in the form of a bard's giving; the two lineages are set side by side, Pari's fame for an absurdly generous gift against Irungovel's descent from the sage's pit and forty-nine generations. Pari's death is never said: the orphaning is carried by யானே தந்தை தோழன், I am the father's friend.

thinai_evidence.note: an offer made to a named chief, carried by praise of his lineage and his giving

202.reading: After the chief has declined, Kapilar reminds him that his ancestors' town Araiyam, rich with wealth heaped in crores, fell because one of them scorned a poem by a wise man of his own kind, then asks pardon for his own foolish words offering Pari's daughters to Evvi's old clan, says he has let the matter go, and wishes the chief's spear victory.
202.nuance: The refusal is never stated; it is read from the poet asking pardon for his own words and saying he has let the girls go. The story of Araiyam is a threat dressed as history: a house that once scorned a poet fell. Reading கழாஅத் தலையை as the name of the scorned poet is ours.

thinai_evidence.note: a poet's parting address to a chief who refused him, closing in a blessing

comparisons.tenor: the boulder strewn with fallen vengai flowers

203.reading: Just as no living thing can live when the sky stops raining and the land hides its yield, it is cruel when a patron answers a bard's 'give again' with 'you took before'; worse than being unable to fill want is to kill the hope of those who come; you are not like that, generous lord who hands bards the enemy's fort as theirs before you take it, since protecting suppliants is your bounden duty.
203.nuance: The poem argues from rain: a sky that stopped because it had already rained would kill all life, so 'you took before' is no reason to refuse. The bard's due is called a debt (பாண்கடன்) and protection of suppliants an ornament the king is bound to wear (பூண்கடன்).

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a giver framed as a plea against refusal

comparisons.tenor: a patron who refuses the bards who come again

204.reading: To say 'give' is low and to refuse is lower still; to say 'take' and give is high and to refuse what is offered higher still; the thirsty do not drink from the clear wide sea but find many paths to a drinking pool, however muddied by cattle and beasts; those who come in hope blame the omens and the hour, never the giver, so I am not angry, Ori, giver who pours like the rain cloud without limit.
204.nuance: The four-step ladder makes refusing a gift the highest act, which quietly ranks the proud bard above the giver. The poet also gives himself a rule of conduct: a disappointed suppliant blames birds and the hour, not the patron.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a named giver after a delay

comparisons.tenor: a great but closed patron set against a small one who gives

205.reading: Even from the three crowned kings of full fortune we do not want gifts given without regard; hunter lord of Kodai, with strong bow and fierce hounds that cut down herds of deer, be free of harm; as the great clouds that gather over the sea do not leave without water, the bards' kin do not leave you without chariots and bright-tusked elephants.
205.nuance: The poem opens with a condition before any praise: honour first, gift second. The cloud image runs the usual figure backwards, since here the bards are the clouds that draw water from the patron's sea.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron through the bard's terms for accepting a gift

comparisons.tenor: the bards' kin who never leave the patron empty-handed

206.reading: Gatekeeper who never shuts the gate on bards who sow bright words in givers' ears: does Anji not know himself, or not know me? The world is not left empty when men of learning and fame die, so we have shouldered our instruments and packed our bags; like the skilled sons of a woodcutting carpenter in a forest, wherever we go, there is rice.
206.nuance: The address is to the gatekeeper, not the king, so the reproach reaches Anji at one remove. The phrase 'he does not know me' sets the bard's rank (வரிசை) against the patron's, and the carpenter's sons make the bard a craftsman who can earn anywhere, not a beggar.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard's proud leave-taking at a patron's gate

comparisons.tenor: the bards who find a living in any land

207.reading: Rise, my heart, let us go: who would call them other than witless, those who see us close yet act as though they did not, and give a gift that does not gladden the heart, with a fallen face? The world is wide and providers many for those who want the honour of 'come'; only those whose spirit sinks, unlike the strong lion, pine over a hard fruit that will never ripen.
207.nuance: The poem distinguishes a gift that makes the face move from one that makes the heart glad (அகம்நக ... முகன்அழி), and the bard refuses the first. The poet speaks to his own heart, as akam speakers do, but the matter is the bard's honour.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard turning from a patron who gave without warmth

comparisons.tenor: the bard who leaves with spirit unbroken

208.reading: When I came past many hills and stood saying I had come to take a gift and go, the guardian sent it out without seeing me, saying 'take this and go'; how did he come to know me? I am not a trading bard for a thing given unseen; even a millet's worth is sweet when givers know the measure of the one they give to and give with care.
208.nuance: The insult is not the size of the gift but that it was given unseen (காணாது ஈத்த): the meeting is part of the gift. The bard calls the alternative trade, so a gift without recognition is a sale.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard rejecting a gift sent without a meeting

209.reading: Lord of a gentle land of fields where the stork rests on the stack and reapers drink toddy from lily leaves and sway to the beat of the waves: like a flock that flew to the fruit tree in the mountain cleft and turns back with nothing when it is bare, shall I who came in hope singing your fame go away empty? Even if you do not give I will not grieve; be well, and may we meet close, at your court of joy where women watch your chest broad as a hill.
209.nuance: The bird simile puts the fault on the bare tree, not the birds, so the patron is told he has gone barren; the refusal to grieve (இரங்குவென் அல்லேன்) and the closing blessing keep the reproach courteous.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard pressing a patron for a delayed gift

comparisons.tenor: the bard leaving the patron empty-handed

210.reading: If kings like you, ignoring your duty to protect the people, are loveless and unjust, our kind should not be born here; my faultless wife, saying that if I were even barely alive I would not fail to think of her and wondering whether unjust Death has made me another's, lives in grief, and to end her pain I give up this waiting; live long, lord: look, I go with a sad heart, my loneliness before me like the guarded fort of your enemies once you have broken it.
210.nuance: The wife's words are quoted inside the bard's, so the reproach to the king is spoken by a woman at home who thinks her husband dead. The final simile is double-edged: the bard is as helpless as the king's beaten enemies, which ranks him with those the king defeats.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard giving up his wait at a patron's court

211.reading: Lord whose army crosses with drums that roar like thunder that splits a snake's head and shakes the hills: when men who would not give said 'he bows to you because you are generous', you achieved your aim; you showed the gift as if it were in my hand and then stood by a lie; though you feel no shame I have said what should shame you, praised you till my tongue ached, worshipped your chest that took fame from being sung, and I go to my bright-browed wife, in a house where even the rat has died for lack of grain, with a son who has forgotten the breast for lack of milk.
211.nuance: The praise is sarcasm the poet names as such (நாணக் கூறி): the king 'achieved what he intended', which was to be praised without paying. The dead house rat is the poem's measure of want, a house too poor even for vermin.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard's ironic praise of a patron who promised and did not give

comparisons.tenor: the roar of the king's drums

212.reading: If you ask who your king is: in a rich land of unending festivals, where field hands drink strong toddy, eat boiled tortoise and roast eel, he is the lord of Kozhi, Kopperuncholan, enemy of the hunger of the bards' kin, who joined Potthi in flawless friendship and gives us great laughter every day.
212.nuance: The speaker, Pisirandhaiyar of the Pandya country, calls the Chola 'our king' (எங்கோ), so the claim of the poem is friendship, not allegiance. The king is named last, after his land's food, and praised for laughter rather than for wealth or war.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a named king's land and friendship

213.reading: Victorious king of the white umbrella: the two who have risen against you are not old enemies, and you are not their enemy either; when you have gained fame and gone to the higher world, what you leave belongs to them; if the young men lose, to whom will your wealth be left, and if you lose to them, only blame remains to please those who scorn you; so give up your fury, rise quickly, keep without confusion the foot-shade that shelters the fallen, for the worthy of the hard-won heaven wait eagerly to receive you as their guest.
213.nuance: The poem never says 'your sons'; the two are only those who came against you (நின்தலை வந்த இருவரை), and the argument works by showing that every outcome is loss: if they die there is no heir, if he loses there is only disgrace. The closing turn to heaven's guests reframes withdrawal from war as the road to a hero's next world.

thinai_evidence.note: counsel to a king who has marched against those who rose against him

214.reading: Those whose minds hold doubt never get past asking 'shall we do good?'; the hunter of elephants gets an elephant while the hunter of quail may come home empty-handed; so if those who aim high get what their deeds earn, they may enjoy the world where no deeds are done; if there is no such joy, they may escape rebirth; and if not reborn, to plant one's fame as high as a Himalayan peak and die in a faultless body is the best.
214.nuance: The argument is a chain of conditionals in which each fallback still pays: heaven, release from birth, or at least lasting fame and a whole body at death. It is spoken by the king himself; the colophon records his authorship, and the poem reads as a reason for the resolve the next poems mourn.

thinai_evidence.note: a king's reasoning about deeds and death, the matter of kaanchi rather than general counsel

comparisons.tenor: those who aim at high deeds and those who aim low

215.reading: In the fine land of the southern hill-lord, where bean-pickers eat their fill of the sour gruel the herd-woman cooks from forked-ear varagu with white velai flowers and white curd, lives Pisiron, they say, the guardian of my life; he may stay away in times of wealth, but in times of trouble he will not stay away.
215.nuance: The king, about to die, praises a poet he has never met as the keeper of his life, and the proof offered is a prediction. The plain mullai food of the friend's land answers the toddy and eel of 212, so each friend praises the other through what is eaten at home.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a friend through his land and his loyalty

216.reading: Do not doubt, wise men, saying that though friends by hearing alone, never having met in many years, it is hard for him to act on it now; he is without scorn, sweet, bound in friendship, wants no lie that would spoil his fame, and when he names himself he says 'my name is the foolish Chola', so close is his claim; he will not stay away at such a time; he will come now; keep his place.
216.nuance: Friendship without meeting is the poem's claim and its wager: the king orders a seat kept for a man he has never seen. The friend's taking the king's own name (பேதைச் சோழன்) is offered as the sign of the bond; that he speaks of the king as 'foolish' is affection, and our reading of who says the name follows the line as it stands.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of an absent friend's faithfulness

217.reading: It is a wonder that a king of such great glory should resolve on this here; a greater wonder that a worthy man of renown from another land should come here at such a time, fame his tradition and friendship his pillar; the greatness of the king who said 'he will come' and the wisdom of the man who came without fail grow past wonder the more one wonders; so what will become of this world that has lost the one who won the heart of a worthy man living where his sceptre did not reach? It is to be pitied.
217.nuance: Three wonders are stacked: the king's resolve, the friend's arrival, and the fulfilled prediction; the lament comes only in the last two lines. The poem treats the friend's coming as the proof of the king's worth: he won a heart beyond the reach of his rule.

thinai_evidence.note: a lament for a dead king, the matter of kaanchi

218.reading: Gold, coral, pearl and the lovely gem of the great hill, though they come from far apart, come together in one place when a precious jewel is strung; so the worthy always fall to the side of the worthy, and the unworthy to the unworthy.
218.nuance: Read in its place after 215 to 217, the jewel stands for the Chola and the Pandya-country poet joined at the end; the poem itself names no one, and its second half (the unworthy join the unworthy) gives the maxim an edge against those who stayed away.

thinai_evidence.note: a general truth drawn from an event, with no lament in the words

comparisons.tenor: the worthy drawn together from distant places

219.reading: Warrior who dries out your whole strong body in the dappled shade on the fork of the river island, you are vexed with me; many indeed are those who sat with you in your resolve.
219.nuance: The four lines carry the whole scene by implication: the king sits on the river island wasting away, others have already joined him, and the poet, arriving late, reads the king's displeasure as being with him. குறிஇருந்தோர் is read as those who sat by his purpose.

thinai_evidence.note: a late-comer's words to a king fasting to death

220.reading: Like the grieving mahout who lost the great tusker that brought him plenty of food and kept him for many years, and weeps to see the empty post in the shed where it stood, was I not shaken when I saw the assembly hall of the famous old town that Killi, giver of chariots with golden garland, has left?
220.nuance: The mahout was fed by the elephant (பெருஞ்சோறு பயந்து), so the simile casts the king as the provider and the poet as his dependant; the empty post (வெளில்) and the empty assembly (மன்றம்) are the poem's two images of absence.

thinai_evidence.note: a lament for a dead king, the matter of kaanchi

comparisons.tenor: the poet before the empty hall of the dead king

links.note: 201 offers Pari's daughters to Irungovel with praise of his lineage; 202, after the refusal, recalls that his ancestors' Araiyam fell for scorning a poet and withdraws the offer.
links.teaches: Read as a pair, the two poems show the bard's praise of lineage working as a bargaining position: the same forty-nine generations that 201 flatters become in 202 a house with a known record of ruin for slighting poets.

links.note: 201 is spoken after Pari's fall, with his daughters taken to another chief; Akananuru 78 measures the heroine's brow by the flowers of the pool of Pari, the giver who drove off kings (வேந்தர்ஓட்டிய).
links.teaches: The akam poet keeps Pari as the victor whose hill still blooms, while Kapilar's poem records the aftermath in which his daughters need a protector, so akam fixes a hero at his height that puram follows past his death.

links.note: 202 closes by wishing Irungovel's spear victory; Akananuru 36 lists Irungo Venman among the seven defeated in one day by Chezhiyan at Alankanam.
links.teaches: If the two name the same house, the akam friend's list of fallen kings shows the defeat that Kapilar's parting blessing does not foresee, and shows akam poets drawing on puram battle-lists as common knowledge to scale a quarrel.

links.note: 203 calls it cruel (இன்னாது) for a patron to refuse a returning bard with 'you took before'; Kural 224 says being asked is itself painful (இன்னாது) to the giver until he sees the asker's glad face.
links.teaches: The same word marks the pain of the asking moment from opposite sides, the giver's in the Kural and the refused bard's in 203, so the couplet's candour about the giver's discomfort is answered by a poet who names what that discomfort costs the asker.

links.note: 204 ranks four acts: asking low, refusing lower, giving high, refusing a gift higher; Kural 222 ranks two: taking is bad even on a good path, giving good even without heaven.
links.teaches: The Sangam poet's ladder adds a rung the Kural lacks, the refusal of what is offered, which shows that the Kural's verdict against taking had a heroic form in which the proud receiver outranks the giver.

links.note: 204 says those who come in hope blame the omens and the hour, never the patron; Kural 1051 says that when the worthy withhold, the blame is theirs and not the asker's. On the plain reading the two place the blame for a refused request in incompatible places.
links.teaches: The bard's courtesy in 204 is a deliberate refusal to lay the blame that the Kural says belongs to the withholder, so the poem shows the decorum that kept a disappointed poet in a patron's favour against the moral rule.

links.note: 204 praises Ori as a giver who pours like the rain cloud without limit; Akananuru 209 names Kari of Mullur, who killed Ori of the strong bow and gave Kolli to the Cheras.
links.teaches: The puram poem preserves Ori as a living patron while the akam friend cites his killing as a famous deed of another chief, so one man's fame survives in the anthologies as both a patron's praise and a rival's trophy.

links.note: 205, by Perunthalai Sathanar, praises the hunter lord of Kodai whose bards never leave without chariots and elephants; Akananuru 13, by the same poet, names the Kodai lord who gives to suppliants without limit (வரைநிலை இன்றி) except the captured elephant.
links.teaches: The same poet turns his patron's giving into an akam measure of what the hero would forgo by leaving, and his akam line keeps a detail the puram poem omits, that one gift, the captured elephant, was only promised by word.

links.note: 205 says the bard does not want even the three kings' gifts if given without regard (பெட்பின்றி); Kural 1057 says the heart rejoices on seeing those who give without scorn.
links.teaches: The Kural states the receiver's joy at a gift given without contempt; 205 turns it into a condition of acceptance, so the manner of giving decided whether a bard would take the gift at all, not only how he felt about it.

links.note: 206 has Avvai leave Anji's gate saying that wherever bards go, there is rice; 207 has Perunchithiranar tell his heart that the world is wide and providers many for those who want honour.
links.teaches: Two poets leaving two patrons reach the same exit, the claim that the world is wide, which shows it was a stock defence of the bard's honour against a patron's slight, not one poet's pique.

links.note: 206 shows the bard leaving in pride when kept waiting at the gate; Kural 1060 says the asker should not be angry when refused, since his own want shows wealth is hard to come by.
links.teaches: Avvai is not refused a gift but denied recognition at the gate, so the pair separates two cases the Kural's counsel of patience joins: want may excuse a refusal, but the bards held that a slight to their rank was not to be borne.

links.note: 207 rejects a gift that does not make the heart glad and leaves the face fallen (அகம்நக வாரா முகன்அழி); Kural 786 says friendship that makes the face smile is not friendship, only that which makes the heart smile.
links.teaches: The Kural's pair of face and heart (முகநக, அகநக) already stands in a bard's test of a gift, so the measure the Kural applies to friendship was first a poet's measure of patronage.

links.note: 208 says the poet is not a trading bard (வாணிகப் பரிசிலன்) for a gift given unseen; 134 says Ay is not a merchant of virtue (அறவிலை வணிகன்) who gives for a return in the next life.
links.teaches: The figure of the trader is used against both sides of the gift: a giver who expects return and a receiver who takes without recognition are both merchants, so the ideal gift was one where neither party was trading.

links.note: 209 likens the bard to birds that leave a fruit tree gone bare; 207 says only the faint-hearted pine for a hard fruit that will never ripen.
links.teaches: Both poets cast the patron as a fruit tree, but 209 blames the tree for being bare while 207 blames the bard for waiting on unripe fruit, so the same image could carry a reproach to the patron or a resolve to leave him.

links.note: Both poems are Perunkunrur Kizhar's to Kudakko Cheral Irumporai; 210 quotes the wife who thinks him dead, 211 ends at the house where the rat has died and the son has forgotten the breast.
links.teaches: The two poems bring the bard's household to the king's court in two ways, the wife's speech in 210 and the bare house in 211, which shows the poor home used as evidence in a bard's case against a patron who kept him waiting.

links.note: 211 tells of a patron who showed the gift as if in hand and then stood by a lie; Kural 1067 begs all who beg not to ask of those who conceal.
links.teaches: The Kural's advice not to beg from concealers is given from outside; 211 shows from inside what the bard does when the advice comes too late, shaming by praise (நாணக் கூறி) as his only remedy.

links.note: 212, by Pisirandhaiyar, praises Kopperuncholan through the toddy, tortoise and eel of his land; 215, by the king, praises Pisirandhaiyar through the varagu, curd and tamarind gruel of his.
links.teaches: Each friend praises the other through the food of the other's home, the Chola's rich marutham fare and the Pandya-country poet's plain mullai fare, so the friendship poems are built as a matched pair across two kingdoms.

links.note: 213 counsels the king that a war with those who rose against him (traditionally his sons) is lost whichever side wins; Kural 889 says inner enmity, though as small as a split sesame seed, holds ruin.
links.teaches: The Kural asserts that enmity within brings ruin; 213 gives the reason in a single case, since in a war inside the house the king loses his heirs if he wins and his honour if he loses.

links.note: 214 urges good deeds on the reckoning that they may win the world without deeds, release from birth, or fame; 134 praises Ay for not being a merchant of virtue who holds that what is done here serves the next life. On the plain reading 214 recommends the very motive 134 scorns.
links.teaches: The same anthology holds a king reasoning openly about the returns of merit and a poet scorning such reasoning in a patron, so the Sangam poets did not share one view of whether a deed's next-world return was a fit motive.

links.note: 214 reasons that even if there is no joy beyond, good deeds may end rebirth or leave fame; Kural 222 says giving is good even if there is no higher world.
links.teaches: Both test good conduct on the supposition that there is no heaven, but the Kural rests there while the king reaches for a further reward, release or fame, so the pair shows two ways of answering doubt about the next world.

links.note: 215 says Pisiron may stay away in prosperity but will not stay away in trouble; Naladiyar 238 is an oath to rush to a friend in distress and put one's life in his hands.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar's oath is a figure of speech, but in the tradition this chapter records the friend did come to share the king's death, so the puram poems supply a case in which the oath was taken literally.

links.note: 216 says the friend, known by hearing alone and never met for many years, will come; Kural 785 says neither meeting nor long acquaintance is needed, feeling alone gives the claim (கிழமை) of friendship.
links.teaches: The Kural's rule and the king's wager share the technical word கிழமை, so the couplet's claim that friendship needs no meeting has a famous royal case behind it, one staked on a seat kept for a man never seen.

links.note: 216 has the king tell doubters that his unseen friend will come; 217 marvels that the king said 'he will come' and the friend came without fail.
links.teaches: The second poem is the fulfilment of the first, and it moves the wonder from the friend's faith to the king's foresight, so the pair shows the lament praising the dead man for having judged a friend rightly.

links.note: 218 says the worthy join the worthy as gems from distant places meet in one jewel; Naladiyar 236 says the water-lily and the kuvalai grow in one pool, yet the small do not equal the great.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar shows that nearness does not make likeness and the Sangam poem that distance does not prevent it, so together they make nature, not place, the ground of fellowship.

links.note: 218 says the worthy fall to the side of the worthy; 219 tells the fasting king that many have already sat with him in his resolve.
links.teaches: The maxim of 218 becomes in 219 a crowd on the river island, which shows that the lament poems treat the number of those who joined the king's death as the measure of his worth.

links.note: 212 shows Kopperuncholan's land of festivals and his daily gift of laughter; 220 shows the assembly of the old town empty after Killi has gone.
links.teaches: Read together, the two poems bracket the Chola's life in the chapter, the festive court of 212 and the empty hall of 220, so the sequence of the anthology itself tells the story of the king's death.

new_concepts.gloss: the gift a bard seeks from a patron, and the asking for it
new_concepts.label_source: the verses use the word: பரிசில் in 206 lines 4-5, 207 line 4, 208 lines 2 and 7, 211 line 7; the colophons of 201 to 211 use it in their thurai

new_concepts.gloss: the helpless grief of those left behind at a patron's or hero's death
new_concepts.label_source: the colophon thurai of 217 to 220 names it

new_concepts.gloss: sitting facing north to fast to death
new_concepts.label_source: the label is ours: 219 shows the king wasting on the river island and those who sat with him; the poems do not use the word

source_issues: 203 line 4: எம்ம்னோர் is a misprint for எம்மனோர்.
206 line 7: அறி யலன்கோல் is a misprint for அறியலன்கொல் (the parallel of என்னறி யலன்கொல் in the same line); line 8: பகழும் is a misprint for புகழும்.

209 line 7: உகத்து. carries a stray full stop and may be a misprint for உகந்து; line 9 ends in a stray full stop. Line 10 is the edition variant the flag records (one edition lacks it), so our text has 19 lines where the review's table counted 18.
201 line 2: the comma is misplaced (அருளித் ,தேருடன்); line 15 is repeated in 202 line 10 (spelt மா அல் and மாஅல்), a formula for Irungovel, not a copying error.
210 line 9: a closing quotation mark ends the wife's speech but no opening mark begins it (it starts at line 5).
214 line 13: the poem ends with a comma (தவத் தலையே,) rather than a close.
218: the poet field reads கண்ணகனார் நத்தத்தனார் எனவும் பாடம், a variant note in the poet field; the review notes the site lacks our line 1, which the simile needs, so all lines are marked.
219: the poet field பெருஞ்கருவூர்ப்சதுக்கத்துப் பூதநாதனார் is misprinted (பெருங்கருவூர்ச் சதுக்கத்துப்).
220 line 1: பெருங்சோறு is a misprint for பெருஞ்சோறு.
213: the colophon thurai துணை வஞ்சி is written as two words; puram_thurai name normalised to துணைவஞ்சி.
